paras: The Moss–Russell affair was a fight in the Congressional library in the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., in the early summer of 1880, in which Lowell Russell, a white Democratic employee, destroyed the Garfield campaign pictures of his Black Republican co-worker John A. Moss and struck him. Moss was dismissed while Russell was restored to duty, and Russell later forfeited collateral on a charge of assaulting Moss. Republican papers treated the librarian's handling of the case as partisan injustice.

Moss and Russell were both employed in the library, which the papers called the Congressional or Capitol library. According to the Monmouth Inquirer, the Black employee had been appointed nine years earlier on the recommendation of Charles Sumner, while the Democrat had been appointed from Virginia six months before. Moss, described as a great admirer of General Garfield, had placed likenesses of Garfield and Arthur, the Republican candidates, over his desk; the Evening Star called the display a Garfield flag.

While Moss was away from his desk, Russell pulled down the pictures and stamped them under his feet, and when Moss replaced them Russell destroyed the second set as well. In the National Republican's account, Russell admitted the act when confronted and asked "What do you propose to do about it?", and Moss answered that it was "a very cowardly act" to destroy his property in his absence. Russell then struck Moss, and in the fight that followed Moss knocked him down. The Evening Star described the encounter only as "a personal altercation" and gave no detail of blows.

The National Republican reported that Spofford, the librarian of Congress, at once dismissed Moss and kept Russell, later granting Russell a leave of absence for July that was understood to be with pay. Russell returned to duty on 1 August while Moss remained out of work. In early August Russell, charged in police court with assault on John A. Moss, forfeited his collateral of $5. No report of any reinstatement of Moss appears in the coverage.

All of the coverage found came from white papers, and most of it from Republican ones. The Washington Evening Star gave the case a short news item headed "The trouble about a Garfield flag in the Capitol library" on 3 August, reporting Moss's complaint that Russell had been restored with back pay, and later listed it among police-court cases as "the Congressional library case." The next day the National Republican ran an editorial, "The Moss and Russell Affair," that called Russell's act an "outrage" and Spofford's response "an act of rank injustice." That editorial said Moss was the more efficient employee but "unfortunately a colored republican, while the aggressor is a white democrat," and read the decision as a sign of the librarian's political sympathies.

Outside Washington, the Monmouth Inquirer of Freehold, New Jersey, told the story without names in a column of Republican campaign paragraphs on 5 August. It argued that the colored man "had only sought to defend himself" and concluded that "the Solid South rules in the Capitol, and Republicans, white and black, must stand aside there." No Black-press report of the affair was found.

The papers differed on the men's status after the fight: the National Republican and the Monmouth Inquirer said Moss was dismissed or discharged, while the Evening Star said both men were suspended. Accounts of Russell's pay also varied, from a July leave "understood" to be paid in the National Republican to restoration "with his back pay" in Moss's complaint as the Evening Star reported it. The police-court disposition is dated 7 August by the Evening Star's same-day report and to the day before 10 August by the National Republican.

reader.title: Moss–Russell affair at the Library of Congress
bases: A single white co-worker destroyed a Black employee's campaign pictures and struck him at their workplace, followed by a police-court assault charge (A1, A2, A4); no mob or group took part.

Two Washington papers (A1, A2) and a New Jersey paper (A3) describe the destruction of the Garfield picture or flag and the fight, and police-court reports in both Washington papers (A4, A5) record Russell's assault charge on Moss.

accounts.label: National Republican editorial
accounts.gist: Russell twice destroyed Moss's Garfield and Arthur likenesses and insolently admitted it; when Moss called it cowardly Russell struck him and got the worst of the scrimmage; Spofford unjustly dismissed Moss and kept Russell.

accounts.label: Monmouth Inquirer editorial
accounts.gist: A Democratic employee from Virginia twice destroyed a colored employee's Garfield picture, struck him when called cowardly, and was knocked down; the colored man was discharged and the white man restored without loss of pay.

accounts.label: Evening Star news item
accounts.gist: Russell tore down Moss's Garfield flag, leading to a personal altercation; both were suspended, and Moss complained that Russell had been restored with back pay.

accounts.label: Police court
accounts.gist: Russell, charged with assault on Moss, forfeited his collateral.

framing.detail: The National Republican's editorial 'The Moss and Russell Affair' called Russell's act an 'outrage' and Spofford's handling 'an act of rank injustice', tying it to Moss being 'a colored republican'.
The Monmouth Inquirer, a Republican paper, said the colored man 'had only sought to defend himself' and closed that 'the Solid South rules in the Capitol'.
The Evening Star ran a brief headed 'The trouble about a Garfield flag in the Capitol library' and later listed the case among police-court dispositions.

conflicts.note: All agree Moss was out of work while Russell was back on duty by early August.
